title.full: The Seventh Carbon Budget: Advice for the UK Government

description: Normative UK pathway to net zero GHG by 2050, including international aviation and shipping.
pathwayDescription:
The Climate Change Committee (CCC) is an independent, statutory body established under the Climate Change Act 2008. Its purpose is to advise the UK and devolved governments on emissions targets and to report to Parliament on progress made in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and preparing for and adapting to the impacts of climate change.
The Balanced Pathway (BP) is the CCC’s normative pathway for the UK to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, covering UK emissions mapped by energy-related sectors, including international aviation and shipping. It underpins the CCC’s advice to set the Seventh Carbon Budget (2038–2042) at 535 MtCO2e and is designed to meet the UK’s 2030 and 2035 NDCs and existing carbon budgets. CO2 emissions reach net zero by 2045, and removals then balance residual methane and nitrous oxide by 2050. The CCC states that net zero by 2050 is consistent with IPCC scenarios that limit warming to 1.5°C, but it does not model a global temperature outcome. Electrification drives the pathway: electricity’s share of final energy demand rises from 17% in 2025 to 69% in 2050, while total final energy demand falls by about 40%. Offshore wind grows from 15 GW to 125 GW and solar from 16 GW to 106 GW, supported by 42 GW of grid storage, 28 GW of interconnection and 38 GW of gas CCS and hydrogen plants, with unabated gas phased out by 2050. Lower demand for high-carbon activities, such as managed growth in flying and dietary change, cuts emissions further, and engineered removals offset what remains. The CCC only includes technologies it expects to reach large-scale use before 2050. Investment averages about £26 billion a year (around 0.9% of GDP), peaking in 2029, and the pathway becomes a net cost saving around 2041. In contrast, emissions in the CCC’s Baseline rise to about 16% above 2023 levels by 2050.

coreDrivers.policies: Phase-out dates for new fossil fuel cars, vans and boilers are key determinants of EV and heat pump roll-out. The Government's high carbon value is built into the cost of flying used to forecast aviation demand, and carbon values set the cost-effectiveness threshold for including measures. Unabated gas generation is phased out by 2050.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Net Zero GHG by 2050 is the binding target. The pathway is built to also meet the 2030 and 2035 NDCs and the Sixth Carbon Budget, and sets the recommended Seventh Carbon Budget (2038-2042) at 535 MtCO2e including international aviation and shipping.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Unit technology costs shape which options enter and when. Measures are included once their abatement cost is below Government carbon values, falling costs from learning rates are projected, and EV uptake depends on purchase price parity, reached for cars and vans in 2026-2028. Where options compete (e.g. DACCS vs synthetic fuel), the cheaper is favoured, though feasibility constraints often bind.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Low-carbon investment rises sharply then falls. Additional capex averages ~GBP 26bn/yr (~0.9% of GDP), equal to 0.73% of GDP in 2025, peaking at 1.84% in 2029, 0.91% in 2040 and -0.06% in 2050 as technology costs fall. Including energy-system expansion (financing requirement) the share is 1.94% at peak and 0.47% in 2050.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population and GDP growth drive demand for transport and aviation in this pathway. In this pathway they are not the main driver; they matter most for aviation, where demand grows faster in the 2040s as GDP rises.
coreDrivers.behavioralShifts: Reduced demand for high-carbon activities is a core lever. Managing aviation demand delivers 54% of aviation abatement in 2040, and lower car travel, modal shift and lower meat and dairy consumption reduce emissions alongside consumer preferences supporting EV uptake. Demand measures are counted before technology measures in the modelling.

dependencies.dependency_description: Rapid grid decarbonisation depends on sustained support.CfD auction funding sufficient to secure required renewables, contracts for new nuclear (6 and BECCS, and CCS and hydrogen business models for low-carbon dispatchable plant.

Planning, consenting and regulatory funding rules limit how fast grids, renewables and CCS can be built. The CCC calls for reform of these processes to enable rapid infrastructure expansion, and flags grid connections as a barrier; Table 2.1 lists planning and regulatory timescales as a key roll-out factor for renewables, grid storage and CCS.

The power transition is capital-heavy and front-loaded. Electricity supply capex peaks at GBP 25bn in 2029 (2023 prices) before turning to savings after 2043. Recent supply-chain inflation raised offshore wind auction prices, though LCOE is still projected to fall to GBP 31/MWh by 2050. Investor confidence depends on market design clarity.

Building transmission and onshore generation raises local acceptance issues. The CCC asks for clear, consistent resolution of tensions between low infrastructure cost and sensitivity to local conditions, favouring overhead lines over undergrounding in most cases. Onshore wind and solar would use about 2% and 1% of UK land.

Consumers must voluntarily offer flexibility: smart demand flexibility grows from 7 GW (2023) to 33 GW (2050) and time-shifted demand to 32 TWh, through EV charging and heat pump operation. This lowers generation and storage needs; less participation would raise system costs.

A decarbonised system relies on networks and flexibility: average transmission boundary capability rises from 5.5 GW to 20.3 GW, interconnection from 10 GW to 28 GW and grid storage from 6 GW to 42 GW by 2050. Low-carbon dispatchable plant needs CCS and hydrogen pipelines and storage. The system is tested hourly against a 1-in-20 weather year.

Firm low-carbon supply relies on technologies not yet at scale: gas CCS and hydrogen turbines (0 to 38 GW by 2050), BECCS power, and medium-duration storage such as compressed/liquid air and flow batteries (7 GW). Battery storage grows tenfold. Technologies below TRL 6 are excluded.

Renewable build needs seabed and land: 81 GW of seabed has been leased, while 2050 solar and onshore wind need about 1% and 2% of UK land. BECCS depends on limited sustainable biomass, with less reliance on imports than in earlier advice.

A weather-dependent system must stay secure through low-wind years and wind droughts, so it is sized to a 1-in-20 adverse weather year. Generation and network assets must be resilient to flooding, storms, extreme heat and reduced water availability, and the CCC asks that resilience be designed in from the outset.
A skilled workforce and supply chain are needed to sustain the renewables pipeline (Table 2.1). Renewables and nuclear could create over 50,000 direct jobs by 2030; no binding shortage is quantified.

Aviation's pathway depends on policy that puts decarbonisation costs into ticket prices, through stronger UK ETS limits or the SAF mandate, and on demand management. Options include a frequent flyer levy and limits on airport expansion. Government may need more demand policy if technology lags, and should push ICAO and CORSIA for higher ambition.

Managing demand relies on decarbonisation costs reaching ticket prices: with full pass-through, a return London-Alicante ticket rises substantially by 2050. SAF and synthetic fuels cost more than DACCS, and feedstock markets will be highly competitive in the late 2020s and 2030s as US, EU and China SAF targets compete.

The CCC's citizens' panel mostly accepted policy-driven ticket price rises, favoured a frequent flyer levy and limits on airport expansion, and wanted annual family holidays protected. This suggests demand management is publicly acceptable if designed fairly.

Demand growth is held to 28% above 2025 passenger numbers by 2050 (402 million), versus 53% per-capita growth by 2040 in the Baseline. This depends on passengers responding to higher prices, with business flight demand growing more slowly and some modal shift to rail.

UK synthetic fuel production from the mid-2030s needs low-carbon hydrogen, captured carbon and CO2 transport and storage. Residual aviation emissions are offset by engineered removals equal to about 60% of UK engineered removals in 2050.

Abatement relies on SAF (38% of liquid fuel by 2050, including synthetic fuel), hybrid-electric and battery-electric aircraft entering from 2040, and efficiency gains of 1.3%/yr. Hydrogen aircraft are excluded as insufficiently developed; the balance between options is uncertain, so all must be pursued.

SAF supply is limited by sustainable biomass and feedstock availability, with strong international competition for feedstock in the late 2020s and 2030s; this is why the SAF trajectory sits below the Government's SAF mandate.

Aviation's non-CO2 effects (mainly contrail cirrus) likely have a large but uncertain warming effect and rise 19% above 2025 by 2050; the CCC asks that they be addressed, but they do not constrain the pathway's measures.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Direct emissions only with EfW and CHP excluded from the sector boundary. No separate captive or rooftop series are included.
UK electricity supply sector, direct (scope 1) emissions in MtCO2e; EfW counted in Waste and CHP in Industry/Fuel supply; average weather year. No separate captive or rooftop series.

Offshore and onshore wind are separated. Grid storage is one figure; battery (35 GW) and medium-duration storage (7 GW) are split but pumped hydro is inside medium-duration. Low-carbon dispatchable combines gas CCS and hydrogen and is classified as Other. Interconnection and demand flexibility shown separately. No captive or rooftop split.

Figures by technology are before  transmission, distribution and storage losses and includes surplus electricity used for electrolytic hydrogen. Imports and exports shown separately and an average weather year is assumed. 'Other' bundles unabated biomass, EfW, hydro and CHP. No captive or rooftop split.

Technology mix is derived as each technology's share of total generation. Figures by technology are before transmission, distribution and storage losses and includes surplus electricity used for electrolytic hydrogen. Imports and exports shown separately and an average weather year is assumed. 'Other' bundles unabated biomass, EfW, hydro and CHP. No captive or rooftop split.

Average transmission network boundary capability (GW) on the boundaries analysed and interconnection capacity. Distribution network needs are described qualitatively. Network reinforcement capex combines both.
Levelised cost of electricity for offshore wind and solar annually; a cost range for low-carbon dispatchable is also provided. Other technologies have no published unit cost.

Additional capex and opex relative to the Baseline (2023 prices), by technology and network reinforcement, for decarbonising and expanding supply. No total investment is provided and it excludes costs already in end-use sectors.
